notes.front: What is cloud native security?
notes.back: An approach that builds security into cloud native applications across their whole lifecycle, from development to production.
notes.explanation: Traditional checks such as last-minute reviews cannot keep up with rapid code changes and short-lived infrastructure; it is closely related to DevSecOps.
notes.example: Scanning each image as it is built and restricting what can run, rather than one security review just before launch.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Cloud Native Security”

notes.front: In the Kubernetes security docs, what are “lifecycle phases”?
notes.back: The stages of an application’s life, from writing code to running it, used to group security controls, following the CNCF cloud native security white paper.
notes.explanation: Each phase has its own risks and controls, so security is applied at every stage instead of only at the end.
notes.example: Code review belongs to the first phase; watching a running Pod’s API access belongs to the last.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Cloud native information security”

notes.front: What is zero trust architecture?
notes.back: A design approach that removes implicit trust: “never trust, always verify”. Components must verify themselves before communicating, even inside the network.
notes.explanation: Traditional networks trust everything inside the perimeter, so one compromised device can reach everything; zero trust treats trust itself as a vulnerability.
notes.example: Two internal services must present certificates to each other before exchanging data, even on the same private network.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Zero Trust Architecture”

notes.front: In a request to the Kubernetes API, what is authentication?
notes.back: The first stage: establishing who is making the request, for example from a client certificate or a token.
notes.explanation: The API server runs one or more authenticator modules in turn until one succeeds; if none does, the request is rejected with HTTP 401.
notes.example: kubectl presents your client certificate, and the API server identifies you as the user “jane”.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authentication”

notes.front: In a request to the Kubernetes API, what is authorization?
notes.back: The second stage: deciding whether the authenticated requester may perform the requested action on the object.
notes.explanation: The request names the user, the action and the object; it is allowed if an existing policy grants that permission, otherwise it is denied with HTTP 403.
notes.example: Jane is authenticated, but a request to delete Pods in namespace prod is refused because no policy lets her.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authorization”

notes.front: What is an admission controller?
notes.back: Code in the API server that checks a create, change or delete request after authorization, before storage, and may modify or reject it.
notes.explanation: Admission controllers may be validating, mutating or both; several Kubernetes features need particular admission controllers enabled.
notes.example: One controller fills in a default value on a new object; another rejects a Pod that breaks a security policy.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”

notes.front: What is RBAC in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Role-based access control: an authorization method where admins grant permissions through roles, configured dynamically through the Kubernetes API.
notes.explanation: It uses four object kinds (Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding) in the rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group.
notes.example: Give the “developers” group read access to Pods in namespace dev by binding a read-only role to that group there.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”

notes.front: In RBAC, what is a Role?
notes.back: A set of permission rules that always applies within one particular namespace.
notes.explanation: When you create a Role you must say which namespace it belongs to. A Role grants nothing until it is bound to someone.
notes.example: A Role in namespace default allowing get, watch and list on Pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: In RBAC, what is a ClusterRole?
notes.back: A set of permission rules that is not namespaced, so it can cover cluster-scoped resources or resources in all namespaces.
notes.explanation: An object is either namespaced or not, never both; that is why Role and ClusterRole are separate kinds.
notes.example: A ClusterRole allowing read access to Nodes, which do not belong to any namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: In RBAC, what is a RoleBinding?
notes.back: An object that grants the permissions of a role to subjects (users, groups or ServiceAccounts) within one namespace.
notes.explanation: ServiceAccounts are identities for workloads, covered shortly. It holds a list of subjects and a reference to the role. It may reference a Role in its namespace, or a ClusterRole to apply it only there.
notes.example: A RoleBinding in namespace dev giving user jane the “pod-reader” Role.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding”

notes.front: In RBAC, what is a ClusterRoleBinding?
notes.back: An object that grants the permissions of a ClusterRole to subjects across the whole cluster.
notes.explanation: Use it when access must apply in every namespace or to cluster-scoped resources.
notes.example: Binding a “secret-reader” ClusterRole to the group “auditors” so they can read Secrets in all namespaces.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding”

notes.front: What is a ServiceAccount?
notes.back: A non-human account that gives processes in Pods, and other workloads, a distinct identity in the cluster.
notes.explanation: Workloads use it to authenticate to the API server and to be granted permissions, for example through RBAC. User accounts, for people, are not API objects.
notes.example: An automation job’s Pod runs as ServiceAccount “deployer”, which a RoleBinding lets update Deployments.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “What are service accounts?”

notes.front: What is a security context?
notes.back: The securityContext field that sets privilege and access-control settings for a Pod or container, such as the user it runs as.
notes.explanation: It can also set Linux security features such as SELinux, AppArmor or seccomp. Set on the Pod spec, it applies to all its containers.
notes.example: securityContext: runAsUser: 1000 makes the container’s processes run as user 1000.
notes.source: Kubernetes glossary, “Security Context”

notes.front: What are the Pod Security Standards?
notes.back: Three policies, each stricter than the last (every level keeps the previous rules and adds more), defining how locked down a Pod must be.
notes.explanation: They are the rules; something else, such as Pod Security Admission, has to enforce them.
notes.example: A Pod that uses the node’s host network (hostNetwork: true) passes the most permissive policy but fails the stricter ones.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”

notes.front: What is Pod Security Admission?
notes.back: The built-in admission controller that enforces the Pod Security Standards, per namespace, when Pods are created.
notes.explanation: You choose the level and the action for each namespace with namespace labels. It has been stable since v1.25.
notes.example: Label a namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline, and Pods breaking the Baseline policy are rejected there.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”

notes.front: What was PodSecurityPolicy?
notes.back: A former Kubernetes API that enforced security restrictions when Pods were created or updated. It has been removed.
notes.explanation: Older study material still teaches it; current clusters use Pod Security Admission or a third-party admission plugin instead.
notes.example: A 2019 tutorial telling you to create a PodSecurityPolicy object will fail on a current cluster.
notes.source: Kubernetes glossary, “Pod Security Policy”

notes.front: Which lifecycle phase aims to keep development environments intact and design applications with good security practice?
notes.back: Develop.
notes.explanation: Suggested measures include a zero trust architecture, security-aware code review, threat modelling and, where justified, fuzzing.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Develop lifecycle phase”

notes.front: Which lifecycle phase secures the supply chain of the container images you run?
notes.back: Distribute.
notes.explanation: Measures include scanning images for known vulnerabilities, encryption in transit, signed artefacts and a private registry for images.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Distribute lifecycle phase”

notes.front: Which lifecycle phase restricts what can be deployed, who can deploy it and where?
notes.back: Deploy.
notes.explanation: It can re-check distribute-phase controls, such as an image’s cryptographic identity, and use namespaces to separate applications.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Deploy lifecycle phase”

notes.front: The Runtime lifecycle phase covers three critical areas. What are they?
notes.back: Access, compute and storage.
notes.explanation: Access means protecting the Kubernetes API (authentication, authorization, TLS); compute and storage cover the running containers and their data.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Runtime lifecycle phase”

notes.front: Develop, Distribute and Runtime are three of the four lifecycle phases. Which one is missing, and where does it fall?
notes.back: Deploy, between Distribute and Runtime.
notes.explanation: The order is Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime: write it, ship it, put it on the cluster, run it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”

notes.front: Older material teaches “the 4C’s of cloud native security” (Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code). How do the current Kubernetes docs frame security instead?
notes.back: By lifecycle phase: Develop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime.
notes.explanation: The 4C’s page existed in the v1.28 docs and has since been replaced by the “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes” page.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation v1.28, “Overview of Cloud Native Security”; current “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: In what order does the API server handle a request’s access checks?
notes.back: Authentication, then authorization, then admission control.
notes.explanation: After TLS is set up, the request is authenticated, authorised and passed through admission controllers; then it is validated and written to the object store.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”

image.alt: Diagram: a human user and a Pod (using a Kubernetes service account) send requests into the Kubernetes API server, where they pass three stages in order, 1 Authentication, 2 Authorization and 3 Admission Control, before step 4 writes to the data store.
image.credit: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API” (diagram of request handling steps)

notes.front: With what HTTP status code does the API server reject a request that cannot be authenticated?
notes.explanation: Authentication modules are tried in sequence; if none succeeds, the request is rejected with 401 (Unauthorized).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authentication”

notes.front: With what HTTP status code is a request rejected when every authorization module denies it?
notes.explanation: If several authorization modules are configured and any one of them authorises the request, it proceeds; only if all deny is it rejected with 403 (Forbidden).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authorization”

notes.front: Does Kubernetes store human users as objects in its API?
notes.back: No. There is no User object; usernames come from authentication and are treated as opaque data.
notes.explanation: ServiceAccounts, by contrast, are API objects. User identities come from outside, for example from client certificates or tokens.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authentication”

notes.front: By default, on which port does the Kubernetes API server listen, protected by TLS?
notes.back: 6443 (production clusters typically serve the API on 443).
notes.explanation: The port can be changed with the --secure-port flag.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Transport security”

notes.front: Which kinds of API request do admission controllers act on?
notes.back: Requests that create, modify or delete objects (and some special actions, such as connect). Never reads: get, watch or list.
notes.explanation: “connect” here means connecting to a Pod through the API server. Reads bypass the admission layer entirely, so admission controllers cannot block them.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “What are they?”

notes.front: Admission control runs in two phases. Which runs first?
notes.back: Mutating admission controllers, then validating ones.
notes.explanation: Mutating controllers may change the object; validating controllers may only accept or reject it. Some controllers do both.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “Admission control phases”

notes.front: If one admission controller rejects a request, what happens to it?
notes.back: The whole request is rejected immediately, and an error is returned to the user.
notes.explanation: Unlike authentication and authorization, where one module saying yes is enough, any admission rejection is final.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Admission control”

notes.front: Which admission controllers let you run your own mutating or validating logic as webhooks?
notes.back: MutatingAdmissionWebhook and ValidatingAdmissionWebhook.
notes.explanation: They call admission webhooks (HTTP calls from the API server to a service you run) configured in the API. MutatingAdmissionPolicy and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy instead embed declarative rules without external calls.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “Admission control extension points”

notes.front: Can an RBAC Role or ClusterRole contain a “deny” rule?
notes.back: No. RBAC permissions are purely additive; there are no deny rules.
notes.explanation: Access is denied simply when nothing grants it; to remove access you remove or narrow a grant.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: What can a ClusterRole grant access to that a Role cannot?
notes.back: Cluster-scoped resources such as Nodes, non-resource endpoints such as /healthz, and namespaced resources across all namespaces.
notes.explanation: A Role is limited to its own namespace; a ClusterRole can also be used for namespaced permissions within particular namespaces.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “ClusterRole example”

notes.front: What happens when a RoleBinding references a ClusterRole?
notes.back: The ClusterRole’s permissions are granted only within the RoleBinding’s namespace.
notes.explanation: This lets you define common permissions once as a ClusterRole and grant them namespace by namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding”

notes.front: What three kinds of subject can a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding name?
notes.back: Users, groups and ServiceAccounts.
notes.explanation: ServiceAccounts are identities for workloads. A binding holds a list of subjects plus a reference to the role being granted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding”

notes.front: A Pod is created without naming a ServiceAccount. Which one does it get?
notes.back: The ServiceAccount named default in the Pod’s namespace.
notes.explanation: Every namespace gets a default ServiceAccount when created; if it is deleted, the control plane recreates it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “Default service accounts”

notes.front: With RBAC enabled, what permissions does a namespace’s default ServiceAccount have?
notes.back: None, apart from the basic right every signed-in identity has to see which APIs exist.
notes.explanation: Any extra access a workload needs must be granted explicitly, for example with a RoleBinding.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “Default service accounts”

notes.front: Is a ServiceAccount namespaced or cluster-wide?
notes.back: Namespaced: each ServiceAccount is bound to one namespace.
notes.explanation: Service accounts are also lightweight and portable, which makes them easy to include in a workload’s configuration.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “What are service accounts?”

notes.front: What is the Privileged Pod Security Standards profile?
notes.back: Unrestricted: the widest permissions, allowing known privilege escalations; meant for trusted system and infrastructure workloads.
notes.explanation: It is defined by the absence of restrictions, so its Pods can bypass normal container isolation, for example by using the node’s host network.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, “Privileged”

notes.front: What is the Baseline Pod Security Standards profile?
notes.back: Minimally restrictive: it prevents known privilege escalations but allows the default Pod configuration.
notes.explanation: It aims at easy adoption for common containerised workloads and non-critical applications.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, “Baseline”

notes.front: What is the Restricted Pod Security Standards profile?
notes.back: Heavily restricted: it enforces current Pod hardening best practice, at some cost to compatibility.
notes.explanation: It targets security-critical applications and lower-trust users; for example, containers must run as non-root.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, “Restricted”

notes.front: From most permissive to most restrictive, the three Pod Security Standards profiles are Privileged, Baseline and {{c1::Restricted}}.
notes.explanation: The policies are cumulative: each step up adds restrictions to the one before.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”

notes.front: In Pod Security Admission, what does the enforce mode do with a Pod that violates the policy?
notes.back: Rejects the Pod.
notes.explanation: Enforce is the only one of the three modes that blocks; audit and warn let the Pod through.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: In Pod Security Admission, what does the audit mode do with a policy violation?
notes.back: Allows the Pod, but records the violation in the API server’s audit log (its record of requests).
notes.explanation: Audit mode leaves a record for administrators without affecting users.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: In Pod Security Admission, what does the warn mode do with a policy violation?
notes.back: Allows the Pod, but returns a warning to the user who made the request.
notes.explanation: Warn mode is useful for showing people what would break before you switch on enforce.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: What namespace label sets the Pod Security Admission level for a mode?
notes.back: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>: <level>, e.g. pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted.
notes.explanation: The mode is enforce, audit or warn; the level is privileged, baseline or restricted. A namespace can set any or all modes, at different levels.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: Does Pod Security Admission’s enforce mode reject a Deployment whose Pod template breaks the policy?
notes.back: No. Enforce applies only to the resulting Pods; audit and warn are also applied to workload resources.
notes.explanation: So the Deployment is accepted but its Pods are rejected; warnings on the Deployment help catch the problem early.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Workload resources and Pod templates”

notes.front: In which versions was PodSecurityPolicy deprecated and removed?
notes.back: Deprecated in v1.21; removed in v1.25.
notes.explanation: Its replacement is Pod Security Admission, or a third-party admission plugin you deploy yourself.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Policies”

notes.front: If you set securityContext at the Pod level (PodSpec.securityContext), which containers does it apply to?
notes.back: All containers in the Pod.
notes.explanation: A security context sets the user and group processes run as, privilege settings, and policies such as SELinux, AppArmor or seccomp.
notes.source: Kubernetes glossary, “Security Context”

notes.front: By default, how are Secret objects stored in etcd, and what should cluster administrators configure?
notes.back: Unencrypted. Administrators should configure encryption at rest for Secret data.
notes.explanation: The base64 encoding of Secret values only obscures them; it is not encryption.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets”, “Configure encryption at rest”; “Secrets”

notes.front: Why is granting list access to Secrets risky?
notes.back: Listing Secrets implicitly lets the subject fetch their contents.
notes.explanation: Good practice is least privilege: restrict watch and list to the most privileged system components, and get to those that need it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets”, “Configure least-privilege access to Secrets”

notes.front: A user cannot read a Secret directly but can create Pods that use it. Can they see its value?
notes.back: Yes. Anyone who can create a Pod using a Secret can see that Secret’s value.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest limiting the impact with short-lived Secrets and audit rules that alert on unusual Secret reads.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets”, “Configure least-privilege access to Secrets”

notes.front: What are the two broad kinds of multi-tenancy in Kubernetes clusters?
notes.back: Multiple teams sharing a cluster, and multiple customers (often called SaaS tenancy).
notes.explanation: Teams usually have some access and some mutual trust; customers usually have no access to the cluster and need strong isolation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Multi-tenancy”, “Use cases”

notes.front: What are the two primary ways to share a Kubernetes cluster between tenants?
notes.back: A namespace per tenant, or a virtual control plane per tenant.
notes.explanation: Namespaces are cheap and well supported but cannot isolate non-namespaced resources; virtual control planes (each tenant gets its own API server and controllers, sharing the worker nodes) can, at a higher resource cost.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Multi-tenancy”, “Implementations”

notes.front: A pipeline scans every container image for known vulnerabilities before it is pushed to a private registry. Which lifecycle phase does this control belong to?
notes.back: Distribute.
notes.explanation: Distribute covers the supply chain of images and artefacts; Deploy then controls what may run where.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Distribute lifecycle phase”

notes.front: Before writing code, a team maps its system’s trust boundaries in a threat model. Which lifecycle phase is this?
notes.back: Develop.
notes.explanation: Develop covers secure design: threat models, security-aware code review and architectures such as zero trust.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Develop lifecycle phase”

notes.front: An administrator turns on TLS for all traffic between nodes and the control plane of a running cluster. Which lifecycle phase does this protect?
notes.back: Runtime (its access area).
notes.explanation: Runtime access protection centres on the Kubernetes API: authentication, authorization and TLS.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Cloud Native Security and Kubernetes”, “Runtime protection: access”

notes.front: A company replaces its one security review before each release with checks built into every stage from coding to production. What approach is this?
notes.back: Cloud native security (closely related to DevSecOps).
notes.explanation: Cloud native security makes security part of the entire lifecycle, suited to rapid change and short-lived infrastructure.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Cloud Native Security”

notes.front: Every internal service must prove its identity to every other service before they exchange data, even inside the private network. What principle is this?
notes.back: Zero trust: never trust, always verify.
notes.explanation: The traditional model trusts anything inside the perimeter; zero trust requires verification for each communication.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Zero Trust Architecture”

notes.front: A user’s kubectl request returns HTTP 403 Forbidden. At which stage of request handling did it fail?
notes.back: B) Authorization.
notes.choices:
A) Authentication
B) Authorization
C) Admission control
notes.choicesExplained: A: a failed authentication returns 401, not 403. C: admission only runs on requests that have already been authorised.
notes.explanation: 403 means the requester was identified but no policy grants the action.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”, “Authorization”

notes.front: A cluster automatically adds a default label to every new Pod before it is stored. What kind of component is doing this?
notes.back: A mutating admission controller.
notes.explanation: Mutating controllers may change the objects they admit; validating ones may only accept or reject them.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “What are they?”

notes.front: A team writes a validating admission webhook to block anyone running kubectl get secrets. Will it work?
notes.back: No. Admission controllers never see read requests (get, watch, list); use RBAC to limit reads.
notes.explanation: Reads bypass the admission layer. Authorization, for example RBAC, is where read access is controlled.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “What are they?”

notes.front: User jane must be able to read Pods in namespace dev only, and no other namespace needs this rule. Which RBAC objects are the simplest fit?
notes.back: A) Role + RoleBinding, both in namespace dev.
notes.choices:
A) Role + RoleBinding
B) ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
C) ClusterRole + RoleBinding
notes.choicesExplained: B would give read access in every namespace. C also works, but adds a cluster-wide ClusterRole, which is only worth it when several namespaces need the same rules.
notes.explanation: A Role sets permissions inside one namespace, and a RoleBinding grants them there.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: A monitoring team needs to list all Nodes in the cluster. Which RBAC objects fit?
notes.back: B) ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.
notes.choices:
A) Role + RoleBinding
B) ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
C) ClusterRole + RoleBinding
notes.choicesExplained: A: a Role is namespaced and cannot cover Nodes, which are cluster-scoped. C: a RoleBinding grants only within one namespace.
notes.explanation: Cluster-scoped resources such as Nodes can only be granted through a ClusterRole bound cluster-wide.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “ClusterRole example”

notes.front: Five teams each need the same “read Secrets” permission, but each only in its own namespace. What is the tidiest RBAC set-up?
notes.back: C) One ClusterRole, bound in each team’s namespace with a RoleBinding.
notes.choices:
A) Role + RoleBinding
B) ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
C) ClusterRole + RoleBinding
notes.choicesExplained: A works but repeats the same Role five times. B would let every team read Secrets in every namespace.
notes.explanation: A RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole grants its permissions only inside the binding’s namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding”

notes.front: An admin wants to add an RBAC rule saying “deny delete on Deployments” for a group that already has edit rights. How is this done?
notes.back: It cannot be: RBAC has no deny rules. Remove or narrow the grant that allows deletion.
notes.explanation: RBAC permissions are purely additive, so access is controlled only by what is granted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: An application in a Pod must read ConfigMaps through the Kubernetes API. What identity should it use, and how does it get permission?
notes.back: A dedicated ServiceAccount, granted access with RBAC, for example a Role and RoleBinding.
notes.explanation: ServiceAccounts give workloads their own identity; the default ServiceAccount has almost no permissions.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “Use cases for Kubernetes service accounts”

notes.front: A nightly backup job and a new engineer both need cluster access. Which should get a ServiceAccount, and which a user account?
notes.back: The backup job gets a ServiceAccount; the engineer gets a user account.
notes.explanation: ServiceAccounts are for workloads and automation and live in the Kubernetes API; user accounts are for people and come from outside.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Service Accounts”, “What are service accounts?”

notes.front: You want the Pod to be required to run as non-root, as the Restricted standard demands. Which field do you set?
notes.back: runAsNonRoot: true, in the container’s (or Pod’s) securityContext.
notes.explanation: A security context holds privilege and access-control settings; the Restricted Pod Security Standard requires running as non-root.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, “Restricted” (Running as Non-root)

notes.front: A node-monitoring agent needs the node’s host network. Which is the only Pod Security Standards profile that allows it?
notes.back: Privileged.
notes.explanation: Baseline and Restricted prevent known privilege escalations such as host access; Privileged has no restrictions.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, “Privileged”

notes.front: Namespace payments has the label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted. Someone creates a Pod whose container runs as root. What happens?
notes.back: Pod Security Admission rejects the Pod.
notes.explanation: Enforce mode rejects violating Pods, and the Restricted profile requires non-root containers.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: Before tightening a namespace to Restricted, you want users to see which of their Pods would fail, without blocking anything yet. Which Pod Security Admission mode do you set?
notes.back: warn (and optionally audit, for a record in the audit log).
notes.explanation: Warn and audit allow the Pod; only enforce rejects it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”, “Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces”

notes.front: A study guide tells you to create a PodSecurityPolicy on your v1.30 cluster. What should you use instead?
notes.back: Pod Security Admission (or a third-party admission plugin): PodSecurityPolicy was removed in v1.25.
notes.explanation: The API no longer exists in current Kubernetes, so the object cannot be created.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Policies”

notes.front: A colleague says Secrets are safe in etcd “because they are base64-encoded”. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
notes.back: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd by default. Enable encryption at rest and restrict access.
notes.explanation: Good practice is encryption at rest for Secret data plus least-privilege RBAC on Secrets and on etcd itself.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets”, “Configure encryption at rest”

notes.front: Tenants on a shared cluster each need their own CustomResourceDefinitions, which are not namespaced. Which multi-tenancy model can isolate them?
notes.back: A virtual control plane per tenant.
notes.explanation: Namespace-per-tenant cannot isolate non-namespaced resources such as CRDs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Multi-tenancy”, “Implementations”

notes.front: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
notes.back: Authentication decides who is making the request; authorization decides whether that identity may do the requested action.
notes.explanation: They run in that order. Failing the first gives 401; failing the second gives 403.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API”

notes.front: What can a mutating admission controller do that a validating one cannot?
notes.back: Modify the object in the request. Validating controllers may only accept or reject it.
notes.explanation: In the first phase, mutating admission controllers run; in the second phase, validating ones do.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Admission Control in Kubernetes”, “What are they?”

notes.front: What is the key difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
notes.back: A Role is namespaced and grants permissions within its namespace; a ClusterRole is not namespaced.
notes.explanation: The same split applies to bindings: a RoleBinding grants within a namespace, a ClusterRoleBinding cluster-wide.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Using RBAC Authorization”, “Role and ClusterRole”

notes.front: What is the difference between the Pod Security Standards and Pod Security Admission?
notes.back: The Standards define the three policy levels; Pod Security Admission is the built-in admission controller that enforces them per namespace.
notes.explanation: Remember: Standards are the rulebook, Admission is the referee.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Admission”

notes.front: How does a security context differ from a Pod Security Standards profile?
notes.back: A security context configures a Pod or container at run time; a profile is a control-plane policy that checks those settings.
notes.explanation: The security context is set in the Pod manifest and passed to the container runtime; the profile decides which settings are allowed.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Pod Security Standards”, FAQ “What’s the difference between a security profile and a security context?”
